source.text: וְ/אִ֨ישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל שָׁ֣בוּ אֶל בְּנֵ֤י בִנְיָמִן֙ וַ/יַּכּ֣וּ/ם לְ/פִי חֶ֔רֶב מֵ/עִ֤יר מְתֹם֙ עַד בְּהֵמָ֔ה עַ֖ד כָּל הַ/נִּמְצָ֑א גַּ֛ם כָּל הֶ/עָרִ֥ים הַ/נִּמְצָא֖וֹת שִׁלְּח֥וּ בָ/אֵֽשׁ־־־־־׃פ
source.note: Diplomatic WLC transcription retained unchanged. The English follows the provisional alternative vocalization recorded in source_interpretation; this is not a claim that WLC itself prints that vowel or that earlier wording has been recovered.

translation.text: And the men of Israel turned back against the sons of Benjamin[a] and struck them with the edge of the sword, from the inhabitants of the cities[b] to livestock, even all that was found. Also all the cities that were found they set on fire[c].

footnotes.text: Hebrew 'sons of Benjamin'; that is, the Benjaminites.

The main text follows an alternative vocalization meaning “city of men,” understood as an inhabited city. The retained WLC transcription instead reads “city of entirety,” also interpreted as the whole city. A published Leningrad transcription correction selects the vowel for “men” but reports both vowel marks. Exact manuscript pointing and earlier wording remain uncertain. “Inhabitants of the cities” interprets the singular city collectively.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Though אִישׁ is singular in form, with a collective sense before a plural verb it functions distributively/collectively. 'The men of Israel' best reflects the masculine, military referent in context and follows the gender-accurate principle better than the more generic 'people of Israel'.
The verb שוב here marks a reversal of movement back toward Benjaminite territory after the battle. 'Turned back' captures the narrative motion more vividly than the flatter 'returned'.

Because the following verb is hostile, English idiom requires 'against' rather than a simple 'to.' 'Sons of Benjamin' preserves the Hebrew kinship expression, though 'Benjaminites' is a viable smoother alternative.

נכה is a broad verb for striking/defeating/slaying. Since the verse then specifies the manner ('with the edge of the sword'), 'struck them' preserves the Hebrew wording without over-specifying beyond the text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the edge of the sword
alternatives: to the mouth of the sword
lexical_decisions.rationale: This is the standard idiom literally involving the 'mouth/edge' of the sword. 'With the edge of the sword' is a natural English equivalent that preserves the concrete imagery better than the more generalized 'by the sword'.

lexical_decisions.source_word: מֵעִיר מְתִם (working vocalization; WLC מֵעִיר מְתֹם)
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the inhabitants of the cities
alternatives: from the entire city (retained WLC pointing)
lexical_decisions.rationale: Explicit provisional source-interpretation choice, not a straightforward gloss of WLC's soundness/entirety noun. The alternative defective plural means men, not dead people; city of men is taken as an inhabited city, with the city expressed collectively. Inhabitants clarifies the human endpoint without limiting it to soldiers. Published correction and lexical/contextual parallels support this working preference; both reported vowel marks, the entire-city alternative and non-discriminating Greek forms prevent a secure codex or historical-priority claim. BDB was consulted; the inherited HALOT label is not a claim of fresh consultation.
The from–to construction extends the selected human-population interpretation to livestock. Preserve the inclusive range; the scope does not independently establish the disputed vowel.
This phrase rounds out the totality of the destruction. 'Even all that was found' preserves the climactic force of עַד while remaining readable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Also all the cities that were found
alternatives: Moreover, all the cities they came upon
And all the cities that remained
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle from מצא likely means the cities encountered/located by the Israelites. 'That were found' is formally close to the Hebrew; a smoother idiom is possible, but this keeps the lexical link with the previous 'all that was found.'
The idiom literally involves 'sending into fire.' 'Set on fire' is clear modern English and avoids archaic phrasing while preserving the action.

revisions.from: And the men of Israel turned back against the sons of Benjamin and struck them with the edge of the sword, from each city, men to livestock, even all that was found. Also all the cities that were found they set on fire.
revisions.to: And the men of Israel turned back against the sons of Benjamin and struck them with the edge of the sword, from the city, men to livestock, all that was found. Also all the cities that were found they set on fire.
revisions.rationale: Changed 'from each city' to 'from the city' to better reflect the singular collective sense of the Hebrew. Removed 'even' for a more natural formal rendering while preserving completeness.

translation.text: And the men of Israel turned back against the sons of Benjamin and struck them with the edge of the sword[a], from each city, men to livestock, even all that was found[c][b]. Also all the cities that were found they set on fire.

footnotes.text: Hebrew 'sons of Benjamin'; that is, the Benjaminites.

The Hebrew phrase rendered 'from each city, men' is difficult. It likely means that they struck down the inhabitants of the cities completely, along with the livestock and everything else found there.

changed_lexical_decisions_before.rationale: The phrase is difficult. מְתֹם likely conveys completeness/wholeness, and in context the sense is that they struck down the inhabitants of the cities completely. Rendering 'from each city, men' makes explicit the implied human referent while preserving the city-by-city scope. The completeness nuance is then carried by the following phrases 'to livestock, even all that was found.'
The עד construction here extends the scope of destruction from humans to animals. 'To livestock' is concise and natural in English.

textual_comparison_history.scope: Published-source interpretation and English clarification; no fresh decipherment.
